alternatives.note: Roster year agrees with the documented date.
One of his own accounts (with Sakhalin as the birthplace), reported by UPI; contradicted by his documented birth in Vladivostok in 1920 and his age of 65 at death.
Given in a film reference under the name Taidje Kahn; rejected for the same reasons.
Roster year agrees with the cited sources.

historical_timeline.summary: Born in Vladivostok, by the documented account; he later gave other birthplaces and years.
First plays the King in The King and I on Broadway; Academy Award for the 1956 film.
Quits smoking after decades of heavy use.
Found to have lung cancer that cannot be removed surgically; treated that month and vows to resume touring.
Last performance as the King in New York, about two years after the diagnosis.
Dies in New York at 65 of complications of cancer; an anti-smoking message he recorded is broadcast after his death.

claims.statement: Yul Brynner was born Yuliy Borisovich Bryner on July 11, 1920, in Vladivostok, Russia.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented date used for the synthetic date of birth; it agrees with his age of 65 at death in contemporary obituaries. He gave other accounts himself (see CLM-0002).

claims.statement: He gave varying accounts of his origins, saying at times that he was born on Sakhalin Island, with the year given as 1915 (UPI gives July 11, 1915; another reference gives July 12, 1915, under the name Taidje Kahn).
claims.clinical_interpretation: The conflicting accounts are his own; they are recorded as rejected alternatives to the documented date.

claims.statement: He first played the King of Siam in The King and I on Broadway in 1951, won the Academy Award for best actor in the 1956 film, and played the role 4,625 times over 34 years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Used for the synthetic modern occupation (stage actor and singer on tour).

claims.statement: He smoked heavily for decades: UPI reported that at one time he smoked five packs of cigarettes a day, and Cancer Today reports two to four packs a day from the age of 12 and that he quit in 1971.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The amounts differ between sources; the quit year is from one source. Used for the former-smoker history; the pack-year estimate in the modern record is synthetic.

claims.statement: In September 1983 he was found to have lung cancer; Cancer Today reports that he had found a lump on his vocal cords and that the tumor was too close to his heart for surgery, and UPI reports that he was treated for lung cancer that month and said he would beat the disease and resume touring.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The diagnosis month and the inoperable tumor are consistent across sources; the voice complaint and the place of treatment are from single sources. Anchors the synthetic presentation with hoarseness and an unresectable left upper lobe cancer.

claims.statement: He returned to the stage and kept playing the King for about two more years; his last performance came in New York in the summer of 1985, less than four months before his death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: UPI gives July 2 for the farewell performance; other accounts give June 30. The case uses summer 1985. Used for the goal of supporting him to keep working.

claims.statement: He said in an interview that he believed his cancer was directly caused by smoking, calling smoking "suicide."

After his death the American Cancer Society released a 30-second television message taken from a January 1985 Good Morning America interview, in which he says: "Now that I'm gone, I tell you: Don't smoke, whatever you do. Just don't smoke."
claims.clinical_interpretation: UPI reports that it first aired on ABC in February 1986, about four months after his death; Cancer Today says networks ran it within days of his death. The case records both and uses neither date in the episode.

claims.statement: He died on October 10, 1985, at 65, at New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center, of complications of cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; after the true-frame episode.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Work up hoarseness from left vocal fold paralysis in a 63-year-old former heavy smoker to a tissue diagnosis of advanced nonsquamous non-small cell lung cancer; stage it with PET-CT and brain MRI; obtain PD-L1 and comprehensive tissue and plasma biomarker testing before choosing first-line systemic therapy (pembrolizumab for PD-L1 70 percent with no actionable alteration); monitor for immune-related adverse events with TSH, free T4, liver tests, glucose, and cortisol as indicated, and evaluate a rash on treatment; start a bone-modifying agent safely; integrate palliative care early (ASCO 2017) with symptom and distress screening; record the tobacco history; begin advance care planning; and support his wish to keep performing, on the CMID lung cancer schedule and NCCN guidance.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Brynner returns two weeks after his first visit. His PET-CT and brain MRI were done eleven days ago, and the endobronchial ultrasound biopsy six days ago. He saw the thoracic oncologist this morning and was told he has adenocarcinoma of the lung that has spread to three bones. His voice is still weak and breathy, and he has not sung since the tour paused. He has a little dry cough in the mornings, no blood in his sputum, and no breathlessness on the level. He has no bone, back, rib, or hip pain, no headache, and no weakness or numbness. His weight is steady. He is sleeping less well with worry, but he says he wants every fact and wants to get back on stage. He has not smoked for 12 years.

assessment_plan.display: Adenocarcinoma of the left upper lobe, stage IVB (cT4 N2 M1c)
assessment_plan.assessment: Tissue diagnosis made: adenocarcinoma, TTF-1 positive, PD-L1 tumor proportion score 70 percent. Staged by PET-CT and brain MRI: mediastinal invasion (T4), aortopulmonary window and subcarinal nodes (N2), and three bone metastases (M1c); no brain metastases. ECOG 1. hpi.narrative: Mr. Brynner is a 63-year-old man with stage IVB adenocarcinoma of the left upper lobe (PD-L1 70 percent, no actionable alteration) who had his second pembrolizumab infusion one week ago and his first zoledronic acid dose the same day. The aches he had for a day after the zoledronic acid dose have gone. He has started no new soap, detergent, or medicine other than the infusions. He has had no diarrhea, abdominal pain, cough, breathlessness, headache, unusual fatigue, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. His voice remains improved since the injection two weeks ago.

documentation.advance_care_planning: Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 30 minutes, with his consent, building on the goals-of-care conversation with the palliative care team. We talked about what metastatic lung cancer can mean, that treatment aims to control it and help him live well for as long as possible rather than to cure it, and why it helps to plan ahead while he is well. He said what matters most to him is to keep working on the stage for as long as he can and to be told the truth plainly. He wants full cancer treatment now. He chose not to record other specific treatment preferences today. The plan will be revisited at the first response scan and at any change in his health.

referral.question: Left upper lobe mass invading the mediastinum with mediastinal nodes and left vocal fold paralysis in a 63-year-old former heavy smoker. Please establish the diagnosis and stage, direct biomarker testing, and advise on first-line treatment
referral.pertinent_history: Six weeks of a weak, breathy voice; he is a stage actor and singer and has paused his tour. Laryngoscopy today: left vocal fold immobile, no laryngeal mass. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis today: 5.2 cm left upper lobe mass invading the aortopulmonary window fat and abutting the aortic arch and left pulmonary artery, enlarged aortopulmonary window and subcarinal nodes, and a small lytic lesion in T10; no adrenal or liver lesion. Mild morning cough, no hemoptysis, no pain, about 2 kg weight loss. ECOG 1. Former smoker: about 3 packs a day from age 12 until he quit 12 years ago (roughly 115 pack-years). Blood count, sodium, potassium, creatinine (eGFR 92), calcium 9.6, liver tests, and glucose normal. PHQ-9 5. PET-CT and brain MRI ordered for this week, and endobronchial ultrasound biopsy requested. He wants plain facts and to return to performing
questions: What is the diagnosis and stage once the PET-CT, brain MRI, and biopsy are done, and is the lytic T10 lesion a metastasis?
Is the biomarker testing complete enough to choose treatment (PD-L1 and comprehensive genomic profiling, tissue and plasma), and should treatment wait for it?
What first-line systemic therapy do you recommend?
Is there a role now for surgery, radiation, or a bone-modifying agent?
What immune-related adverse event monitoring should primary care carry out, and what should prompt a call?
How should palliative care, symptom management, and his wish to keep performing be built into the plan?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Brynner is seen at the request of Dr. Achterberg two weeks after he presented with six weeks of a weak, breathy voice. assessment.assessment: Adenocarcinoma, TTF-1 and napsin A positive, from subcarinal and 4L nodes. The primary invades the mediastinum (T4), the aortopulmonary window and subcarinal nodes are involved (N2), and PET-CT shows avid lytic lesions at T10, the right ilium, and the left sixth rib (M1c, stage IVB). Several typical avid lytic lesions do not need biopsy, because confirming one would not change treatment. The brain MRI is clear. The tumor is not resectable and not curable with surgery or chemoradiation; treatment aims at control, symptom relief, and time

PD-L1 (22C3) tumor proportion score 70 percent. Plasma testing shows no actionable alteration, but a negative plasma result does not exclude a driver, so tissue sequencing (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS G12C, MET exon 14, RET, NTRK, HER2, NRG1) must be reviewed before an immune checkpoint inhibitor is started: starting one before a targetable driver is found can raise the toxicity of later targeted therapy and gives less benefit. The result is expected within a week, so waiting costs little

If no actionable alteration is found, NCCN lists pembrolizumab alone, or pembrolizumab with carboplatin and pemetrexed, among the preferred first-line options for PD-L1 50 percent or more. With ECOG 1, no visceral crisis, and his wish to keep his energy and voice for the stage, pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks is recommended, with chemotherapy added at progression. He has no autoimmune or transplant history that would argue against immunotherapy. After the first response scan, 400 mg every 6 weeks would fit touring

No pain, fracture, or threatened cord, so no radiation is needed now. A bone-modifying agent reduces skeletal events: zoledronic acid 4 mg every 12 weeks after a dental examination, with calcium and vitamin D. Palliative radiation if a lesion becomes painful or threatens fracture
